covenant: Begin the story.
I go down to dinner, introduce myself as Rowan, and take an available place at the table.
I say, "Most recently I earned my keep copying books. I haven't had much practice at being an heir." I help myself to dinner.
I eat and listen to the conversation around me, without trying to take charge of it.
I stay at the table long enough to finish my food and hear what the others are planning for the evening.
If Ashara is still nearby, I ask whether an untrained partner would be any use for practice. If she has already left, I let the opportunity pass.
I accept whatever answer she has given and leave her plans alone. I finish my meal rather than following anyone to practice.
I go to the house library and look on the open shelves for an introductory book about the Council. If I need help finding one, I ask whoever is working there.
Once I have a book, I settle down and read quietly for half an hour.
As I read, I silently wonder whether my aunt once kept a blue glass bird on her desk. I do not say this aloud; it is only a private guess. I return my attention to the page.
I take a short break in the common room. If Seraphel is there and not occupied in a conversation, I ask, "What do you like reading for pleasure?" Otherwise I sit with my book.
If we are talking, I ask Seraphel what she likes about her choice. If she has chosen not to talk, I let her be and read.
I let the conversation end naturally and return to my book. I stay with it until I finish the chapter.
I go to bed when I am done reading. The next morning I wash, dress, and get breakfast in time for the scheduled orientation.
At orientation, I ask how a student in the human seat is supposed to learn the practical duties of the role.
I listen to the answer and then let the next person speak.
After orientation I check the public dueling schedule. If I can watch Ashara's ranked bout, I take a place as a spectator; if it has already finished, I look at the posted result.
Afterward I spend an hour walking in the gardens on my own. I do not seek anyone out.
I return to the common room. If Rashid is there and not busy, I ask how his evening went. Otherwise I leave him to it.
I settle down with my book again. I do not volunteer to sort out anyone else's arrangements.
At the next communal meal I take an available seat. If Seraphel is there, I ask whether she knows a song worth learning; otherwise I listen to the table.
I listen if someone wants to sing or explain the song, without supplying lyrics or a performance of my own. Otherwise I enjoy the meal.
When the meal is over I say goodnight and go back to my room, leaving everyone else to their plans.
The following morning I ask in the library which publicly available records describe the human seat's last active years. I would like to look at the original records if they are open to students.
breakwater: Begin the story.
I go down to the staff supper, introduce myself as Rowan, and take an available place.
I ask Nell what my first day of archive work will involve.
I help myself to food and listen to the conversation around the table.
I ask the person who has been working upstairs what they are working on this evening.
I finish my supper and listen while the others make their plans.
I offer to carry the empty plates back to the kitchen, without offering to take over anybody's work.
If the conversation turns into an argument about who gets to use a room, I listen without deciding for them. I finish clearing away my own things.
I go back to my room and read for twenty minutes, leaving the staff to their own projects.
In private, I consider calling a future short story 'The Red Umbrella'. It is only a possible title: I have not written a story or mentioned the idea to anyone. Then I carry on reading.
I go downstairs for a glass of water and linger in the foyer for a few minutes.
If Owen is around and not busy, I ask whether he recommends any walks for a day off. Otherwise I leave him to his evening.
I thank him if we have been talking, then go upstairs for the night. I do not press anyone for a longer conversation.
I sleep, have breakfast, and arrive for the nine o'clock induction on time. I let Nell begin.
During the induction I ask how to tell what the cinema owns from what is on loan, and what restrictions I need to check before handling an item.

If the loaned photograph album is among the items explained to me, I ask whether one of its photographs could be displayed for the reopening. I do not copy, scan, or publish anything. Otherwise I ask about the permissions on whichever loaned item we are discussing.
I accept the answer about permissions and work within it. I begin the cataloguing tasks I have actually been assigned.
I work quietly through the rest of the morning, putting any loaned material away securely when I stop.
At lunch, if Bea is present, I ask what she enjoys about having the cinema open again. If she is not here, I eat with whoever is around.
I let the conversation finish and go back to the catalogue. I work until the end of my agreed shift.
The following morning I check with Nell for my next archive assignment and any practical changes I need to know about.
I say I am not available for additional front-of-house shifts; I want to keep the hours outside my archive contract for myself.
If Owen is around during a break, I ask how his week is going. If he is not, I take my break without looking for him.
If we have been talking, I tell Owen I will see him tomorrow. Then I take a walk along the harbour on my own.
